title: Area-Information Trade-Offs in Acceleration Radiation from Atoms Falling into Black Holes
authors: Yusef Maleki, Gustavo Valdivia-Mera, Carlos R. Ordonez, Horacio E. Camblong, Marlan O. Scully
abstract: We develop a geometric theory of information processing in the Horizon-brightened acceleration radiation (HBAR) channel, in which the radiative horizon-area change provides an entropy budget for the information carried by the radiation field. Building on the quantum-optical description of atom--field interactions near the horizon and the resulting HBAR thermodynamic correspondence, we derive area-cost laws in the near-steady, thermally saturated regime. The accessible classical information and the mutual information generated between the radiation field and its environment are bounded by the associated radiative horizon-area budget. Reliability is incorporated through Fano's inequality, which translates a prescribed decoding error probability into an area requirement. We further derive Fisher-information speed limits that constrain the statistical evolution of the radiation field and place a lower bound on the duration required for correlation generation. Together, these results establish a bits-per-area principle linking black-hole thermodynamics, information geometry, and quantum information in the HBAR framework.
summary: This work develops an information-theoretic framework for understanding radiation emitted by atoms falling into black holes. It shows that the change in the black hole's horizon area acts as a quantifiable resource budget for the information carried away by the radiation field. Ultimately, it establishes fundamental 'bits-per-area' limits connecting gravity, thermodynamics, and quantum information.
main_problem: The paper develops a geometric theory linking black hole horizon area changes to information processing limits within the Horizon-brightened acceleration radiation (HBAR) channel.
main_result: It establishes a 'bits-per-area principle' that constrains accessible classical information and mutual information based on the radiative horizon-area budget.
method: The analysis combines quantum field theory in curved spacetime with advanced concepts from information geometry, utilizing bounds like Holevo's and Fano's inequalities.
model_or_system: The system involves atoms falling into a black hole described by Kerr geometry, leading to the emission of HBAR. The physics is modeled using quantization of a scalar field ($\Phi$) interacting with the atomic dipole moment.
key_observables: Accessible classical information ($I_{	ext{class}}$), mutual information ($\Delta I_{	ext{M}}$), Fisher Information ($I_F$), and the radiative horizon-area change ($\dot{A}_{	ext{rad}}$).
important_parameters: The analysis focuses on the near-steady, thermally saturated regime; key parameters include the surface gravity ($\kappa$) and angular velocity ($\Omega_H$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the radiative contribution to the horizon area change acts as the geometric resource governing information flow.
paper_structure: The paper builds from a quantum-optical description of atom-field interaction (HBAR) to derive thermodynamic correspondences, then applies information geometry tools (Fisher/Bures lengths) to establish area-cost laws and speed limits on correlation generation.
why_interesting: It provides a deep connection between general relativity (black hole thermodynamics), quantum field theory in curved spacetime, and fundamental principles of quantum information theory, which is highly relevant for theoretical physicists studying open quantum systems near extreme gravitational environments.
